paras: The rape of Henrietta Robinson was an assault on a Black woman by three white men, Maurice Connors, Patrick McNulty and James Reynolds, in the Swampoodle district of northeast Washington, D.C., in the early hours of September 3, 1882. Police arrested all three that night, and in November a jury convicted Connors of rape and found the other two guilty as accessories, a verdict the judge then set aside. The Washington dailies followed the case for nearly four months, and one paper's first headline said it was a case where "Judge Lynch" should have a say.

Robinson, who gave her age as 43, lived with her husband in "Frogtown," south of the Capitol. On the Saturday evening she had gone visiting, to a sister's house in one account and a brother's in another, and on the way home after dark she lost her way in the unfamiliar streets. The Evening Star reported that Connors, 26, had often been arrested, and that McNulty, 23, had been convicted of rape years before and pardoned after two or three years.

About 2 o'clock Sunday morning three white men standing by the Baltimore and Ohio track near F street and Delaware avenue asked her where she was going, and Connors offered to take her home. According to her Police Court testimony, the men seized her and dragged her into a vacant square to the rear of a barn or cow shed, threw her to the ground, and Connors raped her with his hand over her mouth while the others held her. Connors then sent the other two for whisky, saying they would "have a night of it."

Ellen Branch, a Black neighbor, saw three men drag a woman to the shed from her window and called for the police, and a white neighbor also heard the screams. Officers Kaucher and Prather found Connors on the ground holding Robinson and took both to the station house, where she could barely stand from "exhaustion and lameness." Returning to the lot, the officers hid in the shadow of the shed and arrested McNulty and Reynolds when they came back, and Robinson identified them.

On September 4 Judge Bundy of the Police Court sent the case to the grand jury and committed the three for want of bail, given as $3,000 each in most reports and $5,000 in the Evening Critic. On September 30 the prosecutor, C. S. Moore, and Lieut. Kelly told the court that friends of the accused had offered Robinson money to leave town. She admitted being offered money twice but refused to be jailed as a witness because of her family, and Judge Snell, calling her "an honest woman," released her on her own bond.

The grand jury indicted the three for rape on October 12, and at their arraignment on October 16 they pleaded not guilty and were held in $5,000 bail each. At the trial before Judge Wylie on November 15, Connors testified that no force was used and that she had consented, McNulty said she refused him and he never touched her, and Reynolds denied any violence. The jury found Connors guilty as indicted and McNulty and Reynolds guilty as accessories before the fact.

On November 28 Judge Wylie overruled Connors's motion and sentenced him to ten years in the Erie County, New York, penitentiary. He set aside the verdict against the other two, holding that a jury could not find men guilty as accessories under an indictment for rape, and held them in $1,000 bail for the grand jury. The grand jury indicted McNulty and Reynolds as accessories on December 12, and on December 18 they pleaded not guilty while their lawyers insisted they could never be convicted. Judge Wylie replied that there was "a good case" and kept them in jail in default of bail, and no report of a second trial was found.

Three Washington dailies, the Evening Star, the Evening Critic and the National Republican, carried the case from the first hearing through the December arraignment, often on the same day. Their first reports named the attackers' race in the headlines: the Critic's "THREE WHITE BRUTES" said that "Judge Lynch" should have a say, and the Star headlined "THREE WHITE ROUGHS ARRESTED FOR OUTRAGING A COLORED WOMAN." The Critic and the National Republican both called Robinson "a respectable colored woman," and the Star listed the men's police records.

Later coverage read mostly as court reports, though the Critic said much of the trial evidence was "unfit for publication" and ran the defense's plea for release under the headline "A MODEST REQUEST." Brief notices of the verdict and of the motions also ran in the Star and the Critic on November 16 and 20.

The accounts differ on the role of McNulty and Reynolds: the Critic first reported that both tried to rape Robinson, while the Star's account of her testimony said Connors alone did and "the others did not." Robinson's age was given as 43 in her own testimony but as about 55 at trial, and dates of September 1 and "the 4th" in some later reports differ from the September 3 date in the indictment.

reader.title: Rape of Henrietta Robinson
bases: Three named white men were charged with, and one convicted of, raping a Black woman they met on the street; the papers describe a criminal sexual assault by a small group, prosecuted through the courts, not a mob action (A2, A14, A16, A26).

Three Washington dailies independently reported the Police Court hearing, the trial and the conviction, with sworn testimony from the victim, two neighbor witnesses and two policemen (A1, A2, A4, A16, A26).

accounts.label: Defendants' testimony (trial)
accounts.gist: Connors swore there was no force and that she had consented and wanted whisky; McNulty said he solicited her but she refused and he did not touch her; Reynolds denied any violence.

accounts.label: Jury and court
accounts.gist: The jury convicted Connors as indicted and the other two as accessories before the fact; Judge Wylie upheld Connors's conviction but held the accessory verdict invalid under a rape indictment.

framing.detail: The Evening Critic headlined 'THREE WHITE BRUTES,' called Robinson 'a respectable colored woman' and said 'Here Is a Case Where Judge Lynch Should Have a Say'; later it wrote of a 'flendish rape'.
The Evening Star headlined 'A Shocking Crime. THREE WHITE ROUGHS ARRESTED' and recounted the men's police records.
The National Republican called them 'The Outragers' who 'committed the brutal outrage' on 'a respectable colored woman'.
Later trial and sentencing coverage in all three papers was largely court-report prose, though the Critic mocked the defense's 'MODEST REQUEST' for release.
